name: Bill Clinton
summary: Clinton is a centrist Democrat associated with the 'New Democrat' and Third Way approach. He combined fiscal discipline, free trade, welfare-to-work and tough-on-crime policies with support for health coverage, a higher minimum wage, affirmative action, abortion rights, gun limits and climate agreements. He used force for humanitarian ends through NATO, and later in life reversed his positions on DOMA and parts of the 1994 crime bill.

abortion-legal.rationale: Said in 1992 'I am not pro-abortion; I am pro-choice, strongly' and that the decision belongs to women; in 2024 praised Harris's fight for reproductive freedom as backed by a majority.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Said new immigrants must enter the mainstream of American life, learn English and learn about democracy, yet also called America a 'democratic experiment in diversity'; he did not call for giving up original culture.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Signed the 1993 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act, which he called the largest deficit-reduction plan in history, after his own deficit-financed jobs package did not pass.

collective-defense.rationale: Admitted three more countries to NATO, the alliance built on treating an attack on one member as an attack on all.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Defended affirmative action as a means of overcoming the legacy of discrimination ('mend it, don't end it') and launched an initiative on racial opportunity gaps.

death-penalty.rationale: Signed the 1994 crime bill, of which he said the penalty for killing a law enforcement officer would be death, extending the federal death penalty; this covers some but not all of the gravest crimes.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Said the old welfare system undermined the values of work and family and should be a 'second chance, not a way of life'; signed the 1996 law ending the open-ended entitlement. But he also expanded child care and the EITC, and opposed deep cuts, so the evidence is mixed.

decide-locally.rationale: Spoke of shifting decisions from Washington back to states and localities and gave states welfare waivers, but also said some areas, such as illegal immigration, are federal responsibilities.

delink-world-market.rationale: Pushed integration into the world market: NAFTA, China's WTO accession ('we need markets in the world').

democracy-best.rationale: Described democracy and freedom as having 'triumphed' and made democracy promotion a goal; did not address voters choosing badly.

democratic-peace.rationale: Said in 1994 that the best strategy for a durable peace is to support democracy elsewhere because "democracies don't attack each other."

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Asked in 1999 for stronger enforcement of equal pay for equal work and for protection against workplace discrimination, supporting equal rather than distinct legal treatment.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Described America as 'the world's most diverse democracy' that can show people can 'live and advance together' and spoke of building 'One America'.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Argued for opening markets, 240 trade agreements and the global economy, the opposite of a closed bloc.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Brought Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic into NATO, welcoming the Senate vote as strengthening the alliance.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Concluded affirmative action programs should be kept but reformed ('mend it, don't end it'): he rejected rigid quotas and unqualified preferences while opposing abolition.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: In 1999 said discrimination or violence based on race, religion, ancestry, gender, disability or sexual orientation is wrong and ought to be illegal; asked for equal pay and hate crimes legislation.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Said his administration 'did not and will not use rigid quotas to mandate outcomes', favoring equal opportunity and flexible goals.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Called America a nation of immigrants and 'democratic diversity', and welcomed new immigrants as strengthening it.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: In 2012 endorsed Obama's 'all of the above' energy strategy and welcomed the boom in oil and gas production, alongside efficiency and renewables.

force-without-un.rationale: Ordered the 1999 NATO airstrikes on Yugoslavia, which the UN Security Council debate of 24 March 1999 records as taking place without its authorization.

free-trade.rationale: Signed NAFTA, led the China-WTO agreement and boasted of 240 trade agreements; said the US must 'shape this global economy, not shrink from it'.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Said discrimination is wrong and should be illegal, defended enforced anti-discrimination law and asked for protections for parents, women, and others in workplaces.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Signed the 1993 budget law that expanded the earned-income tax credit for working families with children and the working poor, in the signing remarks calling it a way to lift full-time workers out of poverty.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: In Kigali in 1998 he backed the Rwanda tribunal "for as long as it is needed", said all who commit such acts must answer for them, and pledged to work for a permanent international criminal court.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Said in 1997 that 'drugs are wrong, drugs are illegal, and drugs will kill' young people, and signed the largest antidrug budgets; no support for legalization.

limit-growth.rationale: Said the US has always found a way to 'clean the environment and grow the economy at the same time'.

limit-guns.rationale: Signed the Brady Act in 1993 and the 1994 crime bill that banned assault weapons and juvenile handgun ownership; these are significant limits on gun ownership, short of strict ones.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Signed the 1994 crime bill, saying "three strikes and you're out" would be the law of the land for repeat violent offenders.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Mixed: said 'the era of big Government is over' and championed free enterprise and open markets, but also insisted citizens cannot be left to fend for themselves and that government invests in education and health; he did not say markets allocate better than government.

military-superiority.rationale: Said in 1993 'we need a strong military to keep the peace' and sought to keep the US the world's strongest force for peace and freedom.

nation-first.rationale: Said the US must 'shape this global economy, not shrink from it' and that no free nation can enjoy security in isolation; argued for partnerships, NATO and the UN.

national-mission.rationale: Said in 1993 'we will promote our values' and favored democracy abroad; described America as the strongest force for freedom and democracy. Not framed as a 'special mission' to spread its form of government.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Backed a broad role for government in health, education, income support and environment (e.g. Health Security Act, CHIP, Medicare, Brady law).

open-borders.rationale: Increased border controls by 50 percent, hired record numbers of border agents and signed an order against federal contracts to firms hiring illegal immigrants; said 'we are also a nation of laws'.

pay-off-national-debt.rationale: In the 2000 State of the Union he said the country could pay down the national debt entirely in 13 years and be debt-free for the first time since 1835, and asked Congress to stay the course.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: In the 1994 State of the Union he called for resolving "to promote democracy abroad" and named support for the advance of democracy elsewhere the best strategy for security and peace.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Called racial discrimination wrong and illegal, enforced civil rights law and defended affirmative action to overcome its legacy.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Asked Congress in 1995, 1996, 1998, 1999 and 2000 to raise the minimum wage, from $4.25 and then by a dollar over two years; he argued that a modest increase does not cost jobs. A rise of about a dollar is a meaningful but not 'substantial' step, hence +1.

recognise-genocide.rationale: In Kigali in 1998 he named the 1994 killings genocide and regretted that the world had not called them that at once.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Mixed: in 1995-96 stiffened border control, doubled deportations of criminal aliens, and signed measures against illegal immigration, while honoring legal immigrants and calling the US 'a nation of immigrants'. No statement about legal immigration levels.

rehabilitation.rationale: Signed the 1994 crime bill, which made punishment more certain through three strikes, a death penalty for killing police officers and funding for prisons; its prevention money did not change that emphasis.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Signed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, calling religious freedom the most precious of American liberties and requiring government to justify burdens even from general laws.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Repeatedly framed policy as practical ('what works in the real world is cooperation'; builds on 'what works today in the private sector'), avoiding ideological labels.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Signed the Defense of Marriage Act in 1996 with the statement that he had long opposed governmental recognition of same-gender marriages; his later reversal came in words, after he left office, and does not set aside that record.

school-vouchers.rationale: Backed public school choice and charter schools (and in 1992 spoke of choice 'in the public schools they attend'), not public vouchers for any school. His only vouchers were for job training.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Asked Congress in 2000 to fund US participation in reducing the debts of the poorest countries, as urged by the Pope and others. He said 'reduce', so the full cancellation wording is only partly matched.

state-harmful.rationale: Rejected the idea that government is the enemy: described government as 'a progressive instrument of the common good' and said citizens cannot be left to fend for themselves, while seeking a smaller, more efficient one.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Signed the 1993 budget that raised income taxes on the wealthiest Americans; in 1992 asked those earning over $200,000 to pay their 'fair share'; in 2012 attacked tax cuts weighted to upper incomes.

taxation-theft.rationale: Raised income taxes on the wealthy in 1993 and argued for taxes to fund education and health; in 2012 described taxes as a fair means of investing together.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Negotiated NAFTA labor and environmental side agreements, asked that they be enforced, and in 1999-2000 pressed to raise labor standards through the ILO and to elevate labor and environmental issues in the WTO. Whether such standards should be 'binding' in every agreement is less clear.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Proposed the 1993 Health Security Act, under which every American would get a health security card guaranteeing a comprehensive benefit package, financed mainly through employer-based private insurance. Said in 2000 he wanted quality, affordable care for all. Not single-payer, but a state-backed guarantee of coverage.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Signed the 1996 law that cut off many legal immigrants, but from 1997 he repeatedly asked Congress to restore benefits to legal immigrants who work and pay taxes, calling denial 'unworthy of a great nation of immigrants'. Later position wins; he did not argue for illegal immigrants.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Called in 1992 for ending welfare as we know it ('when you can, you must work'); in 1996 signed a law with work requirements and time limits and challenged recipients to take work.

notes: Recent positions govern where he changed: he signed DOMA (1996) but supported same-sex marriage by 2009 and urged DOMA's repeal in 2013; he said in 2015 that the 1994 crime bill's incarceration provisions had overshot. Many answers rest on his presidential speeches (1992-2000) and signed laws; positions he stated only as president may differ from his private views. Items without a quoted or recorded position (e.g. unions, encryption, surveillance, central bank independence, Glass-Steagall as a personal view) are left null. DADT, the 1999 Glass-Steagall repeal and the 1996 Telecommunications Act were signed or accepted under congressional pressure, so they are cited only where a statement matches. Later pass (2026-11-12, rules 7): read all 39 Miller Center speeches and the Gutenberg State of the Union and inaugural texts, searched them by keyword for the statement themes (democracy abroad, international courts, genocide, taxes, crime, guns, privatization, immigration, unions, nuclear weapons and power, campaign finance, military service of gay people), and replaced encyclopedia-based record answers with signing statements and official releases. Themes with no stated position of his in those texts (unions, privatization of pensions, surveillance, encryption, schooling beyond vouchers and charters) stay null.

booksNotUsed.reason: Read or searched by theme with the local corpus tool; these speeches (including State of the Union addresses already cited from the American Presidency Project) added no position needed beyond the sources cited.
